analytic.title: Schedulability Analysis for Distributed Systems Using Network of Action Automata and Environment Automata

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Recently, several formal approaches have been presented to address the problem of schedulability analysis of realtime systems by some varieties of timed automata, e.g., UPPAAL and TIMES. In this paper, we consider a more general and complicated formal computational model for distributed systems. To analyze the schedulability of tasks within this model by automata theory, we present a model, action automata, which is a class of suspension automata, to describe the execution semantics of tasks; we also define an environment model, environment automata, to describe the arrival patterns of tasks. One main result gives the scheduling policies under which the schedulability can be analyzed by our method correctly. To achieve this result, we translate the schedulability analysis to the reachability analysis of the network of action automata and environment automata. Therefore, another main result of this paper is that we prove the reachability of action automata is decidable. Based on these conclusions, we implement a prototype tool for schedulability analysis and test its performance under EDF policy.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: One of the most important issues of real-time systems is to accurately analyze the schedulability in early design stages. Over the years bewildering test techniques have been proposed, for a wide range of scheduling policies and distinct computational models [1]. The schedulability analysis usually considers a worst-case scenario and checks that each task gets a sufficient allocation of shared resources in this situation; if so, then it will also succeed under more favourable circumstances. Since the middle of the 90's, timed automata [2] and some corresponding tools [3], [4] have been used to solve scheduling checking. However, with rapid developments in hardware technology and software engineering, realtime systems are evolving towards much more complicated architectures, such as multi-core or multi-processor distributed systems. Hence, using the existing automata tools to handle such complicated systems has some problems more or less. Motivated by this problem, in this paper we present a new model, action automata, which exactly models execution semantics of tasks distributing on multi-processors. The task execution semantics includes the scheduling relationship between the tasks on the same processor and the activation relationship between the tasks or between the environment and tasks. To describe task request arrivals from environment, we define environment automata to model periodic, sporadic and sporadically periodic tasks. The tasks could even be non-uniform aperiodic tasks as long as their arrival patterns can be modeled by environment automata. Therefore, such a complicated system could be modeled by the parallel composition of environment automata and action automata, and the schedulability analysis is transformed to the reachability analysis of the automata network. In [5], Henzinger proved that the parallel composition of two transition systems, both of which are decidable for their reachability, is still decidable for reachability. The key point of our approach is that we need prove the decidability of action automata.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews the related work, Section III describes our task models. Section IV and Section V define environment automata and action automata respectively. In Section VI we show how to encode the schedulability by reachability, and also give the proof for the decidability of action automata. Section VII concludes the paper.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: To analyze task schedulability, in [6] a timed automaton are used to model all the preemptive possibilities among the tasks explicitly on each hardware component by UPPAAL [4]. Although we could get the checking results by this approach in some simple cases, when task count increases, it becomes very difficult to model the relationship between tasks. To make the schedulability analysis more convenient, task automata and its corresponding tool TIMES [3], has been presented by Fersman et al. [7]. They extend timed automata with bounded subtraction to model some preemptive scheduling policies on a single processor, e.g., rate monotonic scheduling (RMS) and earliest deadline first (EDF). They also show the reachability of timed automata with bounded subtraction is decidable.

There are some other important schedulability analysis approaches besides timed automata: SymTA/S [8] is a compositional analysis approach, which uses so-called standard event models [9] as interface to couple components analysis according to the compositional system level analysis methodology. Thiele et al. present Real-Time Calculus [10] to model any event stream by an appropriate pair of arrival curves and service curves. Perathoner et al. [11] set up some benchmarks to make a direct accuracy comparison of performance analysis methods: MAST approach [12], SymTA/S approach, Real-Time Calculus approach and Timed automata approach. The results show that the analysis approach based on automata provides the most exact performance predictions for all the defined benchmarks, but takes much longer duration than the others. Although both UPPAAL and TIMES can be used to analyze the schedulability of tasks, as mentioned above, a task can not be added into the existing task set by the former easily when modeling a complicated distributed system. The latter leaves the details of adding tasks to be processed at the backstage, and thus saves time for users. But for more complicated tasks, such as sporadically periodic tasks, users still have to model them explicitly by the graphical interface. The biggest restriction of TIMES lies in that all the tasks must be bound on one processor. Therefore, for distributed systems, we can not use TIMES to analyze their schedulability. Therefore, the main motivation of our work is to combine the advantages of both UPPAAL and TIMES, that is, we present an uniform automaton model and tool framework to support schedulability analysis of complicated distributed systems so that the complicated task modeling process is left to backstage and users do not have to have specific formal methods background.

div.head: III. TASK MODEL
div.p: A task T i consists of an infinite number of invocation requests (also called events) from environment or other connected tasks, each of which could be separated by an interval P i and have an initial phase (offset) O i . When a task T i is periodic, its interval P i is equal to a fixed constant; when the task T i is sporadic, its interval P i has a minimum value; when the task T i is sporadically periodic, its interval P i is replaced by two parameters: P e i and P o i , which specify the fixed 'inner' period and minimum 'outer' period respectively [17], and P e i and P o i should satisfy
div.formula: P o i ≥ k * P e i ,
div.p: where k denotes the number of periodic arrival times. Each invocation of task T i is a request to perform a bounded amount of computation C i , i.e., the worst case execution time, which should be completed before its relative deadline D i such that C i ≤ D i . In our model, D i could be greater than, or less than, or equal to P i (or P e i , if task T i is sporadically periodic). Each task can also have a release jitter denoted by J i , which is assumed that we have known a priori. If a task has no buffer to store these requests, the arrival of each request will create a new invocation of this task to be executed, otherwise, its fixed size buffer can receive invocation requests, that is, in this case, there is a sole invocation of this task to exist and the following requests will be stored in the buffer until the buffer is full when its buffer is not empty. When finished, it will check if the buffer is empty. If not, it will delete a request from the buffer, then start a new invocation. When the buffer is full, the newly arrived requests will be dropped.

An example of our model is given in Fig. 1. Tasks T 1 , T 2 and T 4 receive event streams from the environment, called simple activation. Tasks T 3 and T 5 receive event streams generated from tasks T 2 and T 3 respectively, called complex activation. Note that in complex activation the events are generated by the sender only when one invocation of the sender has been completed. IV. ENVIRONMENT AUTOMATA In this section we define a model environment automata, ordinary timed automata [2] essentially, to model the arrival times of task requests from environment directly. The event stream generated by a task will be defined in an action automaton, which will be discussed in Sect. V. We assume a finite events Sync o ranged over by sync o 1 , sync o 2 , ... and a finite set of real-valued clocks X ranged over by x, y, ... We use Φ 0 (X) to denote the set of conjunctive formulas of atomic constraints in the form: x ∼ c, where x ∈ X are clocks, ∼∈ {≤, <, ≥, >}, and c is a natural number.

div.head: VI. ENCODING SCHEDULABILITY
div.p: Each action automaton models a task set bound on one processor. The complex activation pattern between tasks bound on the same processor or bound on the different processors are modeled by the synchronization between the transitions in the same action automaton or in the two different action automata respectively. Unless mentioned explicitly, in the remaining part of this section we concentrate on discussing how to encode the schedulability of tasks bound on one processor by an action automaton A. Note that for each task T i its maximum active invocation number is bounded by a constant W i , which is equal to Di Pi , if task T i is periodic or sporadic, otherwise
div.formula: W i = Di P o i * k,
div.p: where k is the number of periodic arrival times. We introduce a function: state(T ij ) = suspend (arrived, running, or ready) to denote the current semantics status of task invocation T ij (the jth invocation of task T i ) is in suspend (arrived, running, or ready) state respectively.

div.head: A. Task Modeling
div.p: If tasks have no buffer to store their requests, each arrival of requests will create a new invocation of this task to be executed. div.head: Definition 3. (Schedulability) The sets of tasks bound on multiple processors (or a single processor) is schedulable by some scheduling policies, if the environments of tasks is encoded by environment automata, and the execution semantics of tasks and the scheduling policy bound on each processor are encoded into the action automaton, and all the reachable locations in the parallel composition of action automata and environment automata do not contain any sub-location error i .
div.p: We can get the following result:

div.head: Theorem 1. The problem of checking schedulability relative to the scheduling policies that determine which task to be scheduled by neither comparing the elapsed execution time between tasks (resp. task invocations) nor comparing the elapsed execution time of one task (resp. task invocation) with the elapsed relative deadline of another task (resp. task invocation) is decidable.
div.p: Proof: It follows from the definition of transitions in Def. 2 and Corol. 2.
Thus we have the following corollary:

div.head: Corollary 1. The problem of checking schedulability relative to the following scheduling policies: EDF and RMS and DMS and FPS and FIFO on multiple processors is decidable.
div.p: Proof: We can encode any scheduling policy in EDF and RMS and DMS and FPS and FIFO by the guards with no constraint of the form c ic j ∼ c and c id j ∼ c (where c i , c j ∈ C and d j ∈ D and c is a natural number) on transitions in action automata.

div.head: C. Case Study and Performance Evaluation
div.p: In this section, we use again the tasks given in Fig. 1 to illustrate how to model task sets bounded on multiple respectively. In Fig. 3, some guards on transitions are omitted for simplicity. In fact these guards should be defined according to the specific scheduling policies, the function state() is abbreviated as s(), and the range of function state(T i ): suspend, arrived, running and ready are abbreviated as s, a, ru and re respectively. The main obstacle of applying automata theory on schedulability analysis is its relatively poor scalability. In this paper we primarily focus on studying how to use automata theory to analyze schedulability of tasks in complex distributed systems conveniently and expect that future work could improve the test duration using more sophisticated data structure similar to CDD [21] used in UPPAAL. Based on the action automata and environment automata presented in Section IV and V, we have implemented a prototype tool named SCT, in the rest part we only evaluate its performance under EDF due to the space limitation.

We assume that periods are equal to deadlines. Let X be a real interval, we use the symbol '||X||' to denote the finite set composed of f loor(x) for each real number x in X. For example, let X = [1.32, 4.71], we have ||X|| = {1, 2, 3, 4}. The period of each task P i is chosen randomly in the set || [1,30]||, the offset O i and WCET C i are chosen randomly in the set ||[0 * P i , 0.2 * P i ]|| and ||[0.5 * P i /n, 1.5 * P i /n]|| respectively, where n is the current task number. Each point on each curve in the following figure is the average of 100 experiments on a workstation with Intel core2 CPU 4300 1.8GHz and memory 1GB. First we consider the independent periodic tasks. The maximum task count supported by TIMES 1.3 BETA is 8 under EDF policy, the test duration of SCT is close to that of TIMES when task count is between 5 and 8. If there exist n/2 complex activations in the task set, the test duration of SCT decreases since the tasks activated by other tasks have no environment automata, which reduces the state space.

Furthermore, we set up the four benchmarks with the same parameters in [11], for each of which the worst-case response time of the task under test by SCT is the same as that by UPPAAL, which outperforms both holistic analysis and realtime calculus analysis.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: In this paper we study the schedulability analysis for distributed systems by automata theory. The tasks in our model can be complicated under more realistic circumstances. Our technical contributions include that (1) present a class of suspension automata, action automata to model task execution semantics; (2) prove that reachability of action automata is decidable; (3) identify a class of scheduling strategies which can be used in our model to schedule the tasks; (4) implement a prototype tool, which could analyze task schedulability in more complicated real-time systems. However, the number of clocks and timers needed in our approach is still proportional to task invocation count, which in many cases is huge. Therefore a direction of our future work is to reduce the locations and the clocks and timers in some specific cases, then the state
